rv.q: Enough for a nice matinee with a bestie, no?

Whatever charms the 1988 movie had – and they were slight if soggy – have been washed away like so much sand erosion, leaving the stage cluttered with the flotsom of cartoon characters, broadly drawn performances and some chintzy-looking sets.
With the exception of its Cee Cee, alas, almost everything about Beaches is C-minus at best.
It's sad to hear them pour themselves out in service of something so fundamentally trite
Despite all that time and effort, the show is, alas, still not ready for primetime.
For a musical that’s been squatting in various cities for more than 10 years, it’s hard to believe that so many crummy songs litter it.
So it is absolutely bizarre that “Beaches” the musical, which opened on Wednesday night at the Majestic Theater, is a spectacularly unaffecting experience.
Sadly there's little wind beneath this uninspired musical's thin and tattered wings.
Alas, “Beaches” brings only waves of disappointment.

Beaches is that rare new musical based on well-known intellectual property that manages to exceed our hopes, gently sailing us into an ocean of emotional storytelling until we lose sight of the shore.
Beaches is kind of like that, a lovely little show with a sweet heart that's all dolled up for the nearly 2,000-seat Majestic Theatre when it could alight with greater grace somewhere cozier.
"Little Cee" and "Little Bertie," who make appearances throughout the show, ultimately become a highlight of the production.

Still, between its slightly rejiggered character arcs and its handful of engaging tunes, “Beaches: A New Musical” offers more than many screen-to-stage affairs, if not enough to sustain a run time of two and a half hours, including an intermission.
It's perfectly harmless, and just as forgettable.

Unfortunately, the early scenes featuring the youngsters (Samantha Schwartz as the smartass Little Cee Cee and Zeya Grace as the genteel Little Bertie) lack credibility or charm, a problem that largely runs through the entire production.
It’s hard to see why we needed it.
Despite two committed leads, Beaches ultimately drifts away, like sand slipping through the fingers.
As it stands, though, this Beaches is washed-up.

As directed with relatively sure hands by Lonny Price and Matt Cowart and choreographed by Jennifer Rias, the enthusiastic cast rises—and perhaps rises above—the script’s middlingly enthralling script.
Diehard fans of the Bette Midler/Barbara Hershey movie melodrama should be well satisfied, tissues in hand; much audible sobbing could be heard at a recent matinee.
Nor can the musical’s first-rate stars, Jessica Vosk and Kelli Barrett, rescue a vehicle as ill-fated as the Titanic.
A mess as major as “Beaches” required not one but two directors, Lonny Price and Matt Cowart.
The show speed-runs through plot points, including the dissolution of Cee Cee’s marriage to a man she loves (Brent Thiessen) and Bertie’s liberating divorce from a man she doesn’t (Ben Jacoby).
Anyone who has a "best" will find something to love in this wondrously timeless story.

But having Iris Rainer Dart, the original author of the book the movie based on, as the writer here (with the late Thom Thomas) may have doomed the stage version as the show kept too many extraneous plot points that bog down the emotional bond between two lifelong friends.
Jessica Vosk does herculean work, but even a powerhouse performance can't pull Beaches past a forgettable score and a book that both need a major overhaul.
There's not much that's satisfying about the flotsam that's washed up on the shores of the Majestic.
Most of the time Beaches is so painfully dull that one can’t help but wonder how the show got this far.
All in all, Beaches is a profound disappointment.

cn.t: Critics find this long-gestating adaptation mostly waterlogged and misguided, drowning in schmaltz despite strong performances from Jessica Vosk and Kelli Barrett, with only "Wind Beneath My Wings" making a real splash.

sg.ra: Center rows F-L sit just past the first-row neck-crane and just before the Row H mezz overhang bites. Sharp sightlines, clean sound, full set visible from deck to fly loft.
Panoramic top-down view with zero overhang and a steep-enough rake that no head blocks you. The better pick than center orchestra for big choreography or any show with stage-high spectacle.
Steep rake, no one in front of you, nothing cut off. You trade intimacy for a clean full-stage read at roughly a third of center-orchestra pricing.
Priced to move and close to the action, but outer seats clip the far side of the stage and you'll crane for anything upstage. Stay toward the aisle-adjacent seats or accept the compromise.

The front-mezz overhang starts clipping upstage action from Row H and fully buries anything high by Row P. You're paying mid-orchestra prices for a letterboxed view — rear mezz front rows beats this every time.
